title: Tool Selection & Integration
description: A client naming a tool ('an AI chatbot') isn't the same as diagnosing where their process actually breaks — this module trains starting from the workflow, not the tool catalog.

title: Choosing Tools You Can Defend
description: Selecting tools on evidence — cost, exit, support, fit — rather than on category popularity: which layer (existing software, orchestration, RPA, or a model) actually solves the stated need, what a quote leaves out, and what leaving would cost.

title: Designing the Pipeline
description: Specifying an automation as a sequence of steps with defined inputs, outputs and failure behaviour — what each step receives and guarantees, how bursts and overnight batches are handled, what happens to an item that fails halfway, and what runs when the model itself is unavailable.

title: Prompts as Production Components
description: Treating a prompt as a versioned, tested production component rather than a piece of text someone tweaks in a shared doc — structured output the next step can trust, examples that pin down the real edge cases, a version identifier attached to every decision it produced, and a regression test against the full gold set before any revision ships.

title: Integration and the Systems Already There
description: Fitting an automation into the systems a client already runs, without a migration nobody agreed to — treating the existing system as the actual design constraint, matching the integration tier to what it really offers, scoping identity and access deliberately, giving the write-back step the scrutiny it needs, and keeping the manual path alive until the new one has proven itself.

title: Building Something They Can Run Without You
description: Delivering an automation the client's own people can operate, change and turn off — because an automation only the consultant understands is a liability the day the consultant leaves: runbooks written for zero shared context, monitoring that makes failure obvious instead of silent, training aimed at the actual operator, and a real off switch with a named owner.
